video_title: Jason Stanley: Tearing Down Trump’s Propaganda
gist: Philosopher Jason Stanley argues the US has moved from 'soft' persuasive propaganda to 'hard' threat-based propaganda, which he treats as a sign of a shift from liberal democracy to authoritarianism. He expects Trump to try to win the 2026 midterms by undemocratic means, and bots and outrage campaigns to be used to depress Democratic turnout. He also claims tech billionaires are engineering a 'real great replacement' of human labor by AI while blaming immigrants for lost jobs. The episode is political philosophy, not finance, so its market relevance is limited to political, election and institutional risk.

insights.claim: Jason Stanley separates 'soft propaganda', which tries to persuade, from 'hard propaganda', which works through threats and shows of power. He treats a regime's move from the first to the second as a marker that a liberal democracy is becoming authoritarian.
insights.speaker: Jason Stanley
insights.so_what: Gives a qualitative way to monitor political risk in any country: watch whether leaders are trying to persuade people or threatening them.
insights.quote: So, this shift from soft propaganda to hard propaganda is important to attend to.

insights.claim: Stanley argues that Trump has made no attempt to win over voters beyond his base. Instead he threatens political opponents and states that vote Democratic, which Stanley calls hard propaganda aimed at the US's own population.
insights.speaker: Jason Stanley
insights.so_what: If federal power is used to punish Democratic-voting states, federal funding, regulation and enforcement could split along party lines. That is a risk factor for state-level exposures such as munis and regional businesses.
insights.quote: Donald Trump has not sought for a second to broaden his popular support.

insights.claim: Stanley describes 'undermining propaganda' as using an ideal against itself. His main example is the claim of voter fraud: the Trump regime says it is protecting elections while undermining them. He says Republicans already used the claim that undocumented immigrants vote illegally as a strategy by 2015.
insights.speaker: Jason Stanley
insights.so_what: Changes to election rules that are justified as anti-fraud measures are, in Stanley's framework, a warning sign of attempts to undermine elections. They matter for anyone assessing risk around US election outcomes.
insights.quote: Of course, it's the signature undermining propaganda of the Trump regime, which is to say, we're protecting elections.

insights.claim: Stanley borrows Hannah Arendt's distinction between totalitarianism as a movement and totalitarianism in power. A movement depends on a 'central fiction' to justify itself, which for Trumpism is voter fraud. Once in power, it needs less justification and can rely more on threats. On this view Germany's AfD is still a movement, not a party in power.
insights.speaker: Jason Stanley
insights.so_what: Helps separate far-right parties that are only rising in the polls from ones that hold state power when assessing political risk in Europe.

insights.claim: Stanley calls Modi's India a clearer case of authoritarianism than the AfD. He cites India's press-freedom rank of about 154th–157th, just above Belarus and Russia. He says the world still treats India as a democracy only because standards are low for countries with majority non-white populations.
insights.speaker: Jason Stanley
insights.so_what: This disputes the common view of India as a stable democracy. Stanley points to threats of imprisonment for critics, which matters for governance and rule-of-law assumptions in India exposure.

insights.claim: Stanley says the Israel lobby has moved from soft propaganda aimed at American Jews to hard propaganda, such as blacklisting people and making sure student protesters don't get jobs.
insights.speaker: Jason Stanley
insights.so_what: Suggests employer and institutional actions against protesters are becoming a tool of political pressure, which raises reputational and hiring risk for universities and employers.

insights.claim: Stanley argues that Trump and the oligarchs are 'really one thing', that Trump has become an oligarch by enriching himself through the presidency, and that the oligarch class is openly anti-democratic.
insights.speaker: Jason Stanley
insights.so_what: Suggests policy is driven by personal enrichment and politically connected capital, which raises the importance of political access and exposure to rent-seeking.
insights.quote: Trump is himself now an oligarch after having enriched himself uh at the state till

insights.claim: Following Arendt's description of the fascist leader as a mob boss, Stanley says the Trump administration makes loyalty the only test for positions and replaces competent people with loyal ones.
insights.speaker: Jason Stanley
insights.so_what: Picking officials for loyalty over competence lowers state capacity, which raises the risk of policy mistakes at agencies and in security, regulation and economic management.
insights.quote: fascism involves replacing competent people with loyal people.

insights.claim: According to the host, Trump has promised $5,000 payments to American adults if Republicans keep control of Congress. Stanley calls this a bribe, a separate kind of speech act from propaganda. The host adds that it implicitly advertises tariffs as successful enough to pay for the payments.
insights.speaker: Robinson Erhardt (host) / Jason Stanley
insights.so_what: A cash transfer promised on a Republican win is a fiscal and consumer-spending wildcard tied to the midterm result. Watch whether it is funded from tariff revenue.

insights.claim: Stanley predicts Trump will try to win the 2026 midterms by manipulating the system instead of gaining votes. He notes the Supreme Court rejected Trump's attempt to interfere with mail-in voting, but thinks the attempt will still cast doubt on the results.
insights.speaker: Jason Stanley
insights.so_what: Disputed or delegitimized midterm results are a tail risk for US political stability and could raise volatility and policy uncertainty around November 2026.
insights.quote: but he's clearly signaled that he's going to try to to win the midterms by undemocratic means.

insights.claim: Stanley suggests the war in Iran gives Trump another route to an undemocratic midterm win. He sees particular risk if damage to the US security apparatus leads to a terrorist attack on US soil.
insights.speaker: Jason Stanley
insights.so_what: Links geopolitical and security events to election-period politics. A domestic attack before the midterms could be used to justify emergency measures, a scenario worth including in risk plans.

insights.claim: Stanley reads Trump's call for supporters to vote 'as if I'm on the ballot' as aimed at low-propensity voters who turn out only for Trump. In his view it appeals to the 'Trump cult', not the wider Republican base, and not to Democrats.
insights.speaker: Jason Stanley
insights.so_what: Republican midterm results may depend on whether Trump-only voters turn out, a known weakness when Trump is not on the ballot. This is relevant for election-outcome forecasts.

insights.claim: Stanley says bots on social media amplify outrage campaigns. Well-known people post content designed to draw hundreds or thousands of bots into comment threads, which then stirs up real users and keeps outrage constant.
insights.speaker: Jason Stanley
insights.so_what: Measures of social-media sentiment and engagement may be heavily inflated by bots, so treat outrage-driven signals with skepticism.
insights.quote: people on social media are performing for bots

insights.claim: Stanley says Russia's 2016 operation used tens or hundreds of thousands of fake accounts to depress Democratic turnout, for example by targeting Metro Detroit with Hillary Clinton's 'super predator' remark. He expects the same playbook before the 2026 elections, aimed at breaking left-wing solidarity through infighting and Islamophobia.
insights.speaker: Jason Stanley
insights.so_what: Expect coordinated online campaigns to suppress turnout in the weeks before the midterms. This raises uncertainty in polls and turnout models.
insights.quote: That's what happens in the run-up to elections is solidarity is targeted.

insights.claim: Stanley argues that John Stuart Mill's case for free speech depended on norms of mutual respect and not ridiculing people with less power. Because those norms do not hold online, he says Mill's argument fails for social media and face-to-face communication is essential for democracy.
insights.speaker: Jason Stanley
insights.so_what: Supports calls to regulate platforms and challenges the 'free speech' defense used by platform owners, which is a regulatory consideration for social-media companies.
insights.quote: So the whole argument for free speech that Mill gives doesn't work in the online space.

insights.claim: Stanley says Elon Musk's purchase of Twitter, done in the name of free speech, was undermining propaganda. In his view Musk wanted to remove the platform's democratic potential and amplify conspiracy theories. Stanley says he predicted this in Project Syndicate and that many democratically inclined users have since left X.
insights.speaker: Jason Stanley
insights.so_what: Points to lasting user loss and polarization on X among left-leaning users, which matters for its advertising reach and for competitors such as Bluesky.

insights.claim: Stanley says that after 2016, propaganda studies became a technocratic field run by cognitive and social psychologists, and humanists were pushed out. He calls this dangerous because disinformation experts often lack the history needed to recognize tropes such as the Protocols of the Elders of Zion or Great Replacement theory.
insights.speaker: Jason Stanley
entities: Protocols of the Elders of Zion
insights.so_what: Suggests that purely data-driven tools for detecting disinformation will miss propaganda built on historical tropes, a weakness in trust-and-safety and content-moderation approaches.
insights.quote: I started to see a technocratic approach take over to the study of propaganda and I think that's very dangerous.

insights.claim: Stanley endorses Rousseau's remedy for propaganda: reducing social and economic inequality makes people less resentful and less likely to accept scapegoating by fascist politicians. He argues that social media has made the problem much worse.
insights.speaker: Jason Stanley
insights.so_what: Ties economic insecurity directly to how well scapegoating propaganda works, so inequality and job-loss data become leading indicators of political risk.

themes.theme: AI, billionaires and the 'real great replacement'

insights.claim: Stanley claims tech billionaires aim to make most humans unnecessary by replacing them with AI agents, so that they become 'gods' who created a new species. At the same time, he says, they promote the Great Replacement narrative about immigrants taking jobs to hide the fact that AI is doing so.
insights.speaker: Jason Stanley
insights.so_what: Suggests the political backlash to AI job losses may be steered toward immigrants for now but could turn on AI companies and their owners once voters make the connection. That is a regulatory and populist risk for the AI sector.
insights.quote: This is the real great replacement theory

insights.claim: Stanley predicts that billionaires want the security apparatus under firm control before the public realizes AI agents, not immigrants, are taking their jobs. On this account, drones and AI would be used to suppress any rebellion against the billionaire class.
insights.speaker: Jason Stanley
insights.so_what: Points to a link between AI-driven job losses and demand for AI surveillance and autonomous security. Watch political alignment between the defense-tech and AI sectors.

insights.claim: Stanley says Elon Musk wants to become godlike and immortal by helping create an AI 'super species'. He points to Peter Thiel's hesitation when Ross Douthat asked whether humanity should survive as showing how these circles talk. He does not think they want to actively kill people, but says they don't care what happens to humanity.
insights.speaker: Jason Stanley
insights.so_what: Reflects growing hostility from academics and the left toward AI leaders personally, which could feed future political campaigns to regulate or tax AI companies.

insights.claim: Stanley says tech billionaires hide their AI plans by funding far-right parties in many countries that spread Great Replacement theory and fear of migrants and Muslims.
insights.speaker: Jason Stanley
insights.so_what: Suggests far-right electoral gains and tech money are linked across countries, which matters for European and global political-risk scenarios.

insights.claim: Stanley accepts that AI could in principle support democracy, for example as expert input to policy, as his former colleague Robert Post argued about scientists. He concludes that the skeptical case currently far outweighs this.
insights.speaker: Jason Stanley
insights.so_what: Adds to the mainstream academic skepticism about AI's effect on democracy, which feeds pressure for AI regulation.

themes.theme: Speech as affect and social identity

insights.claim: In The Politics of Language, written with linguist David Beaver, Stanley revises semantic theory to show that all speech carries emotional and social-identity content. Propaganda is therefore a spectrum, and the idea of purely informational speech is itself propagandistic.
insights.speaker: Jason Stanley
insights.so_what: Treat official communications such as policy speeches and central-bank or corporate messaging as signals of identity and positioning, not only information.
insights.quote: It's going to be as you say a spectrum because all speech appeals to affect.

insights.claim: Stanley argues that Hillary Clinton's long, wonky policy speeches mainly signaled her identity as a technocratic politician and did little to convey actual policy.
insights.speaker: Jason Stanley
insights.so_what: Shows how to read political messaging for the identity it signals, not only its stated content.

insights.claim: Stanley suggests a way to identify demagogic speech: its emotional charge is out of proportion to the information it carries. His example is the false claim that Haitian immigrants in Springfield were eating cats and dogs, which provokes horror with no factual basis.
insights.speaker: Jason Stanley
insights.so_what: A simple test for any narrative, political or market: if the emotional charge far exceeds the evidence, discount it.

insights.claim: Stanley left Yale for the University of Toronto, where he holds a named chair in American studies. He says being outside the US lets him criticize Trumpism as hard as he wants without drawing attacks onto a US institution. The move cost him about a quarter of his friends and drew criticism from colleagues.
insights.speaker: Jason Stanley
insights.so_what: A prominent example of US academics leaving because of political pressure on universities. It suggests a possible talent drain to Canada and a chilling effect on US institutions.
